reply.title: Why does a sigmoid squash any number into 0 to 1?
reply.story:
When modeling probabilities or neural activations, we often need to take any real number, from negative infinity to positive infinity, and convert it into a neat probability between zero and one. A linear scale will not work because it cannot bound the outputs. We need a smooth, S-shaped curve that compresses extreme values while preserving order.

The standard logistic sigmoid function achieves this by placing an exponential term in the denominator. As the input grows very large and positive, the exponential term shrinks toward zero, pushing the fraction toward one. As the input drops toward negative infinity, the exponential term grows massively, driving the fraction down toward zero.

By adjusting the steepness parameter and the midpoint offset, we can control how sharply the transition happens. The derivative of this curve tells us how sensitive the output is to small changes in the input, reaching its maximum slope right at the midpoint.
reply.cardDescription: Explore how the logistic sigmoid function maps any real number into an output strictly between 0 and 1. Adjust the steepness and midpoint to see how the S-curve bends.
